nodes.name: A degree-$(d+1)$ strategy that passes with probability $1-\frac{1}{m}$
nodes.statement: Fix the polynomial h(x_1, ldots, x_m) = x_1^d+1. Consider the following classical strategy for the degree-d low individual degree test. On a point query u in F_q^m, Prover~A answers a = h(u). On an axis-parallel line query ell = \u + x e_i : x in F_q\, Prover~B returns the restriction hvert_ell when i neq 1, since h is then constant along ell, and returns the zero polynomial when i = 1. The verifier certainly accepts whenever i neq 1, which happens with probability 1 - frac1m. Thus the strategy passes the degree-d test with probability at least 1-eps for eps = frac1m. However, Prover~A is answering according to a polynomial whose individual degree in the first variable is d+1. By Schwartz--Zippel, any polynomial g of individual degree at most d agrees with h on at most a fracd+1q fraction of all inputs, so \[ Prb_u sim F_q^m[g(u)=a] le 1 - meps + fracd+1q. \] This shows that the m-dependent slack in Theorems~ and~ is unavoidable up to polynomial factors.
nodes.raw_latex:
\label{ex:bad-individual-degree-example}
		Fix the polynomial $h(x_1, \ldots, x_m) = x_1^{d+1}$. Consider the following classical strategy for the degree-$d$ low individual degree test. On a point query $u \in \F_q^m$, Prover~$\mathrm{A}$ answers $a = h(u)$. On an axis-parallel line query $\ell = \{u + x e_i : x \in \F_q\}$, Prover~$\mathrm{B}$ returns the restriction $h\vert_{\ell}$ when $i \neq 1$, since $h$ is then constant along $\ell$, and returns the zero polynomial when $i = 1$.

		The verifier certainly accepts whenever $i \neq 1$, which happens with probability $1 - \frac{1}{m}$. Thus the strategy passes the degree-$d$ test with probability at least $1-\eps$ for $\eps = \frac{1}{m}$. However, Prover~$\mathrm{A}$ is answering according to a polynomial whose individual degree in the first variable is $d+1$. By Schwartz--Zippel, any polynomial $g$ of individual degree at most $d$ agrees with $h$ on at most a $\frac{d+1}{q}$ fraction of all inputs, so
		\[
			\Prb_{u \sim \F_q^m}[g(u)=a] \le 1 - m\eps + \frac{d+1}{q}.
		\]
		This shows that the $m$-dependent slack in Theorems~\ref{thm:classical-test-soundness} and~\ref{thm:main-informal} is unavoidable up to polynomial factors.

nodes.name: Low individual degree test
nodes.statement: Fix integers m,d ge 0 and a prime power q. The (m,q,d) low individual degree test has three equally likely subtests. In the axis-parallel lines test, choose a uniformly random role r in \mathrm A,mathrm B\, a uniformly random point u in F_q^m, and a uniformly random coordinate i in \1,dots,m\. Let ell=\u+t e_i : t in F_q\. Player r receives ell and returns a degree-d univariate polynomial fcolon ell to F_q; Player overline r receives u and returns a field element a in F_q. The verifier accepts when f(u)=a. In the self-consistency test, both provers receive the same uniformly random point u in F_q^m and must return the same field element. In the diagonal lines test, choose a uniformly random role r in \mathrm A,mathrm B\, a uniformly random point u in F_q^m, a uniformly random index i in \1,dots,m\, and a uniformly random direction vector v in F_q^m whose last m-i coordinates are 0. Let ell=\u+t v : t in F_q\. Player r receives ell and returns a degree-md univariate polynomial fcolon ell to F_q; Player overline r receives u and returns a field element a in F_q. The verifier accepts when f(u)=a.
nodes.raw_latex:
\label{def:low-individual-degree-test}
	
	
	
	Fix integers $m,d \ge 0$ and a prime power $q$. The $(m,q,d)$ low individual degree test has three equally likely subtests.
	In the axis-parallel lines test, choose a uniformly random role $r \in \{\mathrm A,\mathrm B\}$, a uniformly random point $u \in \F_q^m$, and a uniformly random coordinate $i \in \{1,\dots,m\}$. Let $\ell=\{u+t e_i : t \in \F_q\}$. Player $r$ receives $\ell$ and returns a degree-$d$ univariate polynomial $f\colon \ell \to \F_q$; Player $\overline r$ receives $u$ and returns a field element $a \in \F_q$. The verifier accepts when $f(u)=a$.
	In the self-consistency test, both provers receive the same uniformly random point $u \in \F_q^m$ and must return the same field element.
	In the diagonal lines test, choose a uniformly random role $r \in \{\mathrm A,\mathrm B\}$, a uniformly random point $u \in \F_q^m$, a uniformly random index $i \in \{1,\dots,m\}$, and a uniformly random direction vector $v \in \F_q^m$ whose last $m-i$ coordinates are $0$. Let $\ell=\{u+t v : t \in \F_q\}$. Player $r$ receives $\ell$ and returns a degree-$md$ univariate polynomial $f\colon \ell \to \F_q$; Player $\overline r$ receives $u$ and returns a field element $a \in \F_q$. The verifier accepts when $f(u)=a$.

Let ell=\u+t e_i : t in F_q\. Player r receives ell and returns a degree-d univariate polynomial fcolon ell to F_q; Player overline r receives u and returns a field element a in F_q. The verifier accepts when f(u)=a. In the self-consistency test, both provers receive the same uniformly random point u in F_q^m and must return the same field element. In the diagonal lines test, choose a uniformly random role r in \mathrm A,mathrm B\, a uniformly random point u in F_q^m, a uniformly random index i in \1,dots,m\, and a uniformly random direction vector v in F_q^m whose last m-i coordinates are 0. Let ell=\u+t v : t in F_q\. Player r receives ell and returns a degree-md univariate polynomial fcolon ell to F_q; Player overline r receives u and returns a field element a in F_q. The verifier accepts when f(u)=a.

nodes.name: Heterogeneous role-register unsymmetrization
nodes.statement: Let \(psi\) be a normalized bipartite state on \(mathcal H_mathrm Aotimesmathcal H_mathrm B\), let \(M^mathrm A\) and \(M^mathrm B\) be projective measurements on the two prover spaces with a common outcome type, and let \(G\) be an arbitrary measurement on the heterogeneous role-register space \[ \mathrm A,mathrm B\times(mathcal H_mathrm Aoplusmathcal H_mathrm B). \] After applying the direct-sum role-register symmetrization, the consistency defect between the symmetrized point measurement and \(G\) is the average of the two defects obtained from the occupied principal blocks of \(G\). nodes.name: Good-strategy characterization
nodes.statement: Using notation which will be introduced in Chapter~ below, a symmetric strategy is (eps,delta,gamma)-good if and only if it satisfies the following three conditions. For ell and u as in the axis-parallel lines test, \[ A_a^u ot I simeq_eps I ot B^ell_[f(u)=a], and A_a^u ot I simeq_delta I ot A_a^u. \] And for ell and u as in the diagonal lines test, \[ A_a^u ot I simeq_gamma I ot L^ell_[f(u)=a]. \]
nodes.raw_latex:
\label{rem:good-strat-characterization}
	Using notation which will be introduced in Chapter~\ref{chap:preliminaries} below, a symmetric strategy is $(\eps,\delta,\gamma)$-good if and only if it satisfies the following three conditions. For $\ell$ and $u$ as in the axis-parallel lines test,
	\[
		A_a^u \ot I \simeq_\eps I \ot B^\ell_{[f(u)=a]},

		\quad
		A_a^u \ot I \simeq_\delta I \ot A_a^u.
	\]
	And for $\ell$ and $u$ as in the diagonal lines test,
	\[
		A_a^u \ot I \simeq_\gamma I \ot L^\ell_{[f(u)=a]}.
	\]

nodes.name: Restricted diagonal lines test
nodes.statement: Consider the (m,q,d) low individual degree test. For j in \1,dots,m\, the j-restricted diagonal lines test is the diagonal lines test conditioned on i=j. In particular, the m-restricted diagonal lines test is the diagonal lines test in which the sampled line is a uniformly random line in F_q^m.

	Consider the $(m,q,d)$ low individual degree test. For $j \in \{1,\dots,m\}$, the $j$-restricted diagonal lines test is the diagonal lines test conditioned on $i=j$. nodes.name: Quantum soundness of the low individual degree test
nodes.statement: Let (psi, A^mathrm A, B^mathrm A, L^mathrm A, A^mathrm B, B^mathrm B, L^mathrm B) be a projective strategy that passes the (m,q,d) low individual degree test with probability at least 1-eps. Let \(k>0\) be an integer with \(k ge 400md\), and set \[ nu = 100000 k^2 m^4left(eps^1/40000 + (d/q)^1/40000 + e^-k/(2560000m^2)right). \] Then there exist projective measurements G^mathrm A, G^mathrm B in polymeasmqd with the following properties: item on average over u sim F_q^m, \[ A_a^mathrm A,u ot I simeq_nu I ot G^mathrm B_[g(u)=a], I ot A_a^mathrm B,u simeq_nu G^mathrm A_[g(u)=a] ot I; \] item \[ G_g^mathrm A ot I simeq_nu I ot G_g^mathrm B. \]
assumptions: Let (psi, A^mathrm A, B^mathrm A, L^mathrm A, A^mathrm B, B^mathrm B, L^mathrm B) be a projective strategy that passes the (m,q,d) low individual degree test with probability at least 1-eps.
Let \(k>0\) be an integer with \(k ge 400md\), and set \[ nu = 100000 k^2 m^4left(eps^1/40000 + (d/q)^1/40000 + e^-k/(2560000m^2)right).

\] Then there exist projective measurements G^mathrm A, G^mathrm B in polymeasmqd with the following properties: item on average over u sim F_q^m, \[ A_a^mathrm A,u ot I simeq_nu I ot G^mathrm B_[g(u)=a], I ot A_a^mathrm B,u simeq_nu G^mathrm A_[g(u)=a] ot I; \] item \[ G_g^mathrm A ot I simeq_nu I ot G_g^mathrm B.
nodes.raw_latex:
\label{thm:main-formal}
	
	
	
	Let $(\psi, A^{\mathrm A}, B^{\mathrm A}, L^{\mathrm A},
	A^{\mathrm B}, B^{\mathrm B}, L^{\mathrm B})$ be a projective strategy that
	passes the $(m,q,d)$ low individual degree test with probability at least
	$1-\eps$. Let \(k>0\) be an integer with \(k \ge 400md\), and set
	\[
		\nu = 100000 k^2 m^4\left(\eps^{1/40000} + (d/q)^{1/40000} + e^{-k/(2560000m^2)}\right).
	\]
	Then there exist projective measurements
	$G^{\mathrm A}, G^{\mathrm B} \in \polymeas{m}{q}{d}$ with the following
	properties:
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item on average over $u \sim \F_q^m$,
		      \[
			      A_a^{\mathrm A,u} \ot I \simeq_\nu I \ot G^{\mathrm B}_{[g(u)=a]},
			      \qquad
			      I \ot A_a^{\mathrm B,u} \simeq_\nu G^{\mathrm A}_{[g(u)=a]} \ot I;
		      \]
		\item
		      \[
			      G_g^{\mathrm A} \ot I \simeq_\nu I \ot G_g^{\mathrm B}.
		      \]
	\end{enumerate}

Let \(k>0\) be an integer with \(k ge 400md\), and set \[ nu = 100000 k^2 m^4left(eps^1/40000 + (d/q)^1/40000 + e^-k/(2560000m^2)right). \] Then there exist projective measurements G^mathrm A, G^mathrm B in polymeasmqd with the following properties: item on average over u sim F_q^m, \[ A_a^mathrm A,u ot I simeq_nu I ot G^mathrm B_[g(u)=a], I ot A_a^mathrm B,u simeq_nu G^mathrm A_[g(u)=a] ot I; \] item \[ G_g^mathrm A ot I simeq_nu I ot G_g^mathrm B. \]

nodes.name: Two-space role-register reduction for the source theorem
nodes.statement: The printed final theorem starts from a projective strategy on two possibly different local Hilbert spaces. The source proof uses the role-register symmetrization and then unsymmetrizes the polynomial measurement. Lean formalizes this reduction for the general two-space source strategy. The trace-level factor-two unsymmetrization estimate for arbitrary heterogeneous role-register measurements is formalized in Lemma~. The heterogeneous role-register symmetrization may be fed into the source-shaped main-induction theorem under the corrected large-\(k\) hypothesis \(kge 400md\), and the resulting role-register consistency estimate can be unsymmetrized into the two point-consistency estimates on the original two-space strategy with the expected factor \(2\). The remaining steps of the source-boundary passage are also checked. The point-agreement branch is available for the paper-faithful two-space strategy, and the Schwartz--Zippel Step~5 theorem has been generalized from the same-space carrier to a bipartite state on \(H_Aotimes H_B\). The heterogeneous triangle/SDD comparison theorem gives the complete-measurement full-polynomial consistency statement at the end of the paper's Step~5 calculation. The two heterogeneous orthonormalization applications produce projective submeasurements on the two local Hilbert spaces, and the completion step widens the resulting left- and right-factor state-dependent-distance estimates to the orthonormalize-and-complete error appearing in the paper. The repaired polynomial line-169 consistency relations use the Cauchy--Schwarz loss from the pre-completion orthonormalization estimates, not a new hypothesis. The final point-evaluation triangle postprocesses these relations and the completed \(Q_A,Q_B\) projective consistency estimate by evaluation at a point, combines them by the heterogeneous triangle inequality, and absorbs the explicit pre-absorption errors into the final \(nu=mainFormalError\) bound under the nonzero scalar-cascade boundary \(0<k\). This is the small-error branch used in the corrected two-space source theorem, where \(k>0\) is part of the theorem statement.

nodes.raw_latex:
\label{lem:good-strategy-characterization}
	
	
	
	A symmetric projective strategy $(\psi,A,B,L)$ is $(\eps,\delta,\gamma)$-good if and only if the following hold on the relevant test distributions:
	\[
		A_a^u \ot I \simeq_\eps I \ot B^{\ell}_{[f(u)=a]},
		\qquad
		A_a^u \ot I \simeq_\delta I \ot A_a^u,
		\qquad
		A_a^u \ot I \simeq_\gamma I \ot L^{\ell}_{[f(u)=a]}.
	\]

nodes.raw_latex:
\label{def:approx_delta}
	
	
	Let $\ket{\psi} \in \mathcal H$, let $A=\{A_a^x\}$ and $B=\{B_a^x\}$ be families of operators on $\mathcal H$, and let $\mathcal D$ be a distribution on the question set. We write
	\[
		A_a^x \approx_\delta B_a^x
	\]
	when
	\[
		\E_{x \sim \mathcal D} \sum_a \lVert (A_a^x-B_a^x)\ket{\psi} \rVert^2 \le \delta.
	\]

nodes.raw_latex:
\label{prop:simeq-to-approx}
	
	
	
	If $A$ and $B$ are measurements and $A_a^x \ot I \simeq_\delta I \ot B_a^x$, then
	\[
		A_a^x \ot I \approx_{2\delta} I \ot B_a^x.
	\]

nodes.statement: By Lemma~, \[ sum_a lVert(A_a-C_a)ot I ketpsi rVert^2 leq 2delta + 2 cdot lVert(I-B)ot I ketpsirVert^2. \] It remains to bound the residual term. Since 0 le I-B le I, lVert(I-B) ot I ketpsirVert^2 & leq 1 -sum_a brapsi B_a^2 ot I ketpsi. By Proposition~, \[ sum_a brapsi B_a^2 ot I ketpsi approx_sqrtdelta sum_a brapsi (A_a B_a)ot I ketpsi approx_sqrtdelta sum_a brapsi A_a^2ot I ketpsi. \] Proposition~ gives \[ sum_a brapsi A_a^2ot I ketpsi geq brapsi A ot I ketpsi - zeta = 1-zeta. \] Hence implies \[ lVert(I-B) ot I ketpsirVert^2 le 2sqrtdelta + zeta. \] Substituting this into the first bound proves the claim.

By Lemma~\ref{prop:triangle-inequality-for-vectors-squared},
	\[
		\sum_a \lVert(A_a-C_a)\ot I \ket{\psi} \rVert^2
		\leq 2\delta + 2 \cdot \lVert(I-B)\ot I \ket{\psi}\rVert^2.
	\]
	It remains to bound the residual term. Since $0 \le I-B \le I$,
	\begin{align}
		\lVert(I-B) \ot I \ket{\psi}\rVert^2
		 & \leq 1 -\sum_a \bra{\psi} B_a^2 \ot I \ket{\psi}.
		\label{eq:to-return-later-whatevs}
	\end{align}
	By Proposition~\ref{prop:easy-approx-from-approx-delta},
	\[
		\sum_a \bra{\psi} B_a^2 \ot I \ket{\psi}
		\approx_{\sqrt{\delta}} \sum_a \bra{\psi} (A_a B_a)\ot I \ket{\psi}
		\approx_{\sqrt{\delta}} \sum_a \bra{\psi} A_a^2\ot I \ket{\psi}.
	\]
	Proposition~\ref{prop:cool-prop} gives
	\[
		\sum_a \bra{\psi} A_a^2\ot I \ket{\psi} \geq \bra{\psi} A \ot I \ket{\psi} - \zeta = 1-\zeta.
	\]
	Hence \eqref{eq:to-return-later-whatevs} implies
	\[
		\lVert(I-B) \ot I \ket{\psi}\rVert^2 \le 2\sqrt\delta + \zeta.
	\]
	Substituting this into the first bound proves the claim.

Since 0 le I-B le I, lVert(I-B) ot I ketpsirVert^2 & leq 1 -sum_a brapsi B_a^2 ot I ketpsi. \label{thm:naimark}
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	Let $\ket{\psi}$ be a state in $\mathcal H_{\mathrm A} \ot \mathcal H_{\mathrm B}$.
	Let $A = \{A^x_a\}$ be a sub-measurement acting on $\mathcal H_{\mathrm A}$
	and $B=\{B^y_b\}$ be a sub-measurement acting on $\mathcal H_{\mathrm B}$.
	Then there exist Hilbert spaces $\mathcal H_{\mathrm A_{\mathsf{aux}}}$ and $\mathcal H_{\mathrm B_{\mathsf{aux}}}$,
	a state $\ket{\mathsf{aux}} \in \mathcal H_{\mathrm A_{\mathsf{aux}}} \ot \mathcal H_{\mathrm B_{\mathsf{aux}}}$,
	and projective sub-measurements $\widehat{A} = \{\widehat{A}^x_a\}$ and $\widehat{B}=\{\widehat{B}^y_b\}$
	acting on $\mathcal H_{\mathrm A} \ot \mathcal H_{\mathrm A_{\mathsf{aux}}}$
	and $\mathcal H_{\mathrm B} \ot \mathcal H_{\mathrm B_{\mathsf{aux}}}$, respectively,
	such that, if $\ket{\widehat{\psi}} = \ket{\psi} \ot \ket{\mathsf{aux}}$, then for all $x,y,a,b$,
	\[
		\bra{\psi} A^x_a \ot B^y_b \ket{\psi}
		=
		\bra{\widehat{\psi}} \widehat{A}^x_a \ot \widehat{B}^y_b \ket{\widehat{\psi}}.
	\]
	In addition, $\ket{\mathsf{aux}}$ is a product state.
	The word ``measurement'' in the source statement is read here in the
	projective-submeasurement sense used by Lemma~\ref{lem:naimark-helper}: for a
	general sub-measurement, the residual mass is carried by the additional
	\(\bot\) outcome in the auxiliary construction, so the original outcomes need
	not sum to the identity.

	projective sub-measurement $\widetilde A^x$. Do the same for each question $y$
	on Bob's side, obtaining auxiliary states $\ket{\mathsf{aux}_{\mathrm B,y}}$
	and projective sub-measurements $\widetilde B^y$.

	Let
	\[
		\ket{\mathsf{aux}}
		=
		\Big(\bigotimes_x \ket{\mathsf{aux}_{\mathrm A,x}}\Big)
		\ot
		\Big(\bigotimes_y \ket{\mathsf{aux}_{\mathrm B,y}}\Big),
		\qquad
		\ket{\widehat{\psi}} = \ket{\psi} \ot \ket{\mathsf{aux}},
	\]
	and let $\widehat A^x_a$ and $\widehat B^y_b$ be obtained by letting
	$\widetilde A^x_a$ or $\widetilde B^y_b$ act on the relevant auxiliary factor
	and the identity act on every other auxiliary factor. Because the auxiliary

		=

	\]

nodes.statement: The checked Lean proof of Theorem~ uses the standard one-measurement auxiliary register \[ Option(mathcal A), \] with the all-\(bot\) vector as the initial auxiliary state. \label{thm:orthonormalization}

		A_a \ot I \approx_{100 \zeta^{1/4}} P_a \ot I.
	\]

nodes.statement: Lean exposes the quantitative obstruction at the projectivization transition used in the inductive step. The existing line-156 transition gives only the generic consequence of Proposition~: from G^mathrm Asimeq_zeta_1G^mathrm B and G^mathrm Aapprox_zeta_2Q^mathrm A one obtains Q^mathrm Asimeq_zeta_1+sqrtzeta_2G^mathrm B, and similarly on the other tensor factor. This direct square-root-loss route is an immediate specialization of the general Lean declarations MIPStarRE.LDT.Preliminaries.triangleSub and MIPStarRE.LDT.Preliminaries.triangleSub\_right to the handoff fields, and is no longer maintained as separate named projectivization API. Lean also proves a more local repaired transport that keeps the comparison at the pre-completion stage. If P^mathrm A is the orthonormalized projective sub-measurement with G^mathrm Aapprox_epsilonP^mathrm A, then Proposition~ bounds the diagonal match-mass loss by sqrtepsilon, and canonical completion can only add nonnegative diagonal match mass. Thus the declarations leftConsistency\_of\_completion\_and\_sdd and rightConsistency\_of\_completion\_and\_sdd prove Q^mathrm Asimeq_zeta_1+sqrtepsilonG^mathrm B and its Bob-side mirror from the pre-projective zeta_1 consistency plus the pre-completion approx_epsilon comparison. This is much sharper than the direct completion-level zeta_1+sqrtzeta_2 route, but it is still not the paper's exact zeta_1. Lean also isolates the completion fact used inside this sharper repair: the canonical completion of a projective submeasurement can only increase its diagonal match mass against a fixed partner submeasurement. The sharper route therefore pays its square-root loss before completion and then uses completion only in this monotone direction, with no additional match-mass penalty. The older exact-zeta_1 construction-level monotonicity statement has been retired. The current Section~5 API proves the checked repaired transport above, and the active orthonormalization route now uses those repaired completion-transport estimates rather than a separate exact match-mass witness.

Consider an orthonormal basis for $\C^{k+1}$ consisting of vectors $\ket{a}$ for $a \in \mathcal A$ and the vector $\ket{\bot}$. Let $U$ be any unitary such that for each vector $\ket{\phi}$,
	\[
		U \cdot (\ket{\phi} \ot \ket{\mathsf{aux}})
		=
		\sum_{a \in \mathcal A} ((A_a)^{1/2}\ket{\phi}) \ot \ket{a}
		+
		((I-A)^{1/2}\ket{\phi}) \ot \ket{\bot},
	\]
	where $A=\sum_a A_a$. Then
	\[
		U \cdot (I \ot \ket{\mathsf{aux}})
		=
		\sum_{a \in \mathcal A} (A_a)^{1/2} \ot \ket{a}
		+
		(I-A)^{1/2} \ot \ket{\bot},
	\]
	so for any $a \in \mathcal A$,
	\[
		(I \ot \bra{a}) \cdot U \cdot (I \ot \ket{\mathsf{aux}})
		=
		(A_a)^{1/2}.
	\]

		 & =
		(A_a)^{1/2} \cdot (A_a)^{1/2}

nodes.name: Naimark dilation does not preserve $\approx_\delta$
nodes.statement: Let ketpsi be any state in C^d ot C^d, and consider the two-outcome measurements A = \A_0, A_1\ and B = \B_0, B_1\ with \[ A_0 = A_1 = B_0 = B_1 = tfrac12 I. \] For each outcome a in \0,1\, the operators A_a ot I and I ot B_a are both equal to tfrac12 I ot I, so A_a ot I approx_0 I ot B_a on the state ketpsi. Now apply the Naimark construction with a qubit auxiliary space on each side and auxiliary state ket+ = tfrac1sqrt 2(ket0+ket1). Since A and B are genuine measurements rather than sub-measurements, the extra ketbot direction from is unnecessary in this example. The unitary from can then be taken to be the identity, so the dilated measurements are \[ widehat A_a = I ot ketabraa, widehat B_a = I ot ketabraa. \] If ketwidehatpsi = ketpsi ot ket+ ot ket+, then a direct calculation gives \[ sum_a in \0,1\ bigllVert (widehat A_a ot I - I ot widehat B_a) ketwidehatpsi bigrrVert^2 = 1. \] Thus on the state ketwidehatpsi the dilated family satisfies widehat A_a ot I approx_delta I ot widehat B_a only for delta ge 1, even though the original family satisfied the same relation with delta = 0. This is why we use Theorem~ rather than simply applying Theorem~: Naimark preserves the outcome probabilities, but it need not preserve the state-dependent approx_delta estimates needed later.

			A_0 = A_1 = B_0 = B_1 = \tfrac{1}{2} I.

	Remark~\ref{rem:lean-orthonormalization-main-declarations}.  Let

The strong self-consistency assumption implies \[ brapsi A ot A ketpsi geq brapsi A ot I ketpsi - zeta, \] so \[ brapsi A ot (I-A) ketpsi leq zeta. \] Rearranging once more gives \[ brapsi (I-A) ot (I-A) ketpsi geq brapsi (I-A) ot I ketpsi - zeta. \] Complete \(A\) to the measurement \(widehat A=\widehat A_a\_a in widehatmathcal A\) on \(widehatmathcal A=mathcal A cup \bot\\) by setting \(widehat A_a=A_a\) for \(a in mathcal A\) and \(widehat A_bot=I-A\). Adding the two preceding inequalities shows that \(widehat A\) is \(2zeta\)-strongly self-consistent. By , this gives the source almost-projective estimate \[ sum_a brapsi bigl((widehat A_aot I)-(widehat A_aot I)^2bigr) ketpsi le 4zeta. \] Apply to obtain a projective sub-measurement \(widehat P\) such that \[ widehat A_a ot I approx_84(4zeta)^1/4 widehat P_a ot I. \] Discard the extra outcome and set \(P_a=widehat P_a\) for \(a in mathcal A\). Write \(A=\sum_a A_a\).  The strong self-consistency assumption implies
	\[
		\bra{\psi} A \ot A \ket{\psi}
		\geq
		\bra{\psi} A \ot I \ket{\psi} - \zeta,
	\]
	so
	\[
		\bra{\psi} A \ot (I-A) \ket{\psi} \leq \zeta.
	\]
	Rearranging once more gives
	\[
		\bra{\psi} (I-A) \ot (I-A) \ket{\psi}
		\geq
		\bra{\psi} (I-A) \ot I \ket{\psi} - \zeta.
	\]

	Complete \(A\) to the measurement
	\(\widehat A=\{\widehat A_a\}_{a \in \widehat{\mathcal A}}\) on
	\(\widehat{\mathcal A}=\mathcal A \cup \{\bot\}\) by setting
	\(\widehat A_a=A_a\) for \(a \in \mathcal A\) and
	\(\widehat A_{\bot}=I-A\).  Adding the two preceding inequalities shows
	that \(\widehat A\) is \(2\zeta\)-strongly self-consistent.  By
	\ref{prop:other-two-notions-of-self-consistency}, this gives the source
	almost-projective estimate
	\[
		\sum_a \bra{\psi}
		\bigl((\widehat A_a\ot I)-(\widehat A_a\ot I)^2\bigr)
		\ket{\psi}
		\le 4\zeta.
	\]
	Apply \ref{lem:locality-preserving-projectivization} to obtain a projective
	sub-measurement \(\widehat P\) such that
	\[
		\widehat A_a \ot I \approx_{84(4\zeta)^{1/4}} \widehat P_a \ot I.
	\]
	Discard the extra outcome and set \(P_a=\widehat P_a\) for
	\(a \in \mathcal A\).  Then
	\[
		A_a \ot I \approx_{84(4\zeta)^{1/4}} P_a \ot I,
	\]
	and \(84 \cdot 4^{1/4} \leq 120\), so the completion-route bound follows.

nodes.name: Proof of \ref{lem:orthonormalization-main-lemma}
nodes.statement: The statement is trivial when zeta > 1/4, so assume zeta leq 1/4. By , \[ sum_a brapsi A_a ot B_a ketpsi geq 1-zeta. \] Apply Cauchy--Schwarz to \[ sum_a brapsi (A_a ot I)cdot(I ot B_a)ketpsi \] to obtain \[ sum_a brapsi (A_a)^2 ot I ketpsi geq (1-zeta)^2 geq 1-2zeta. \] Because A is a measurement, this rewrites as sum_a brapsi (A_a-(A_a)^2) ot I ketpsi leq 2zeta. For any x in [0, 1], (x - trunc_delta(x))^2 leq frac1delta cdot (x - x^2). If x geq 1-delta, then trunc_delta(x)=1. Since delta leq 1/2 below, one also has x geq delta, so \[ (x-trunc_delta(x))^2 = (1-x)^2 leq (1-x)fracxdelta = frac1delta(x-x^2). \] If x < 1-delta, then trunc_delta(x)=0, and similarly \[ (x-trunc_delta(x))^2 = x^2 leq xfrac1-xdelta = frac1delta(x-x^2). \] [Rounding to projectors] There exists a set of projective matrices \R_a\ such that A_a ot I approx_2sqrtzeta R_a ot I. and R:= sum_a R_a leq (1+2sqrtzeta) cdot I. Write the eigendecomposition of A_a as \[ A_a = sum_i lambda_a,iketu_a,ibrau_a,i. \] Choose 0 < delta leq 1/2, define trunc_delta:[0,1] to \0,1\ by trunc_delta(x)=1 when x geq 1-delta and 0 otherwise, and set \[ R_a = trunc_delta(A_a) = sum_i trunc_delta(lambda_a,i) ketu_a,ibrau_a,i. \] By , \[ (A_a-R_a)^2 leq frac1delta(A_a-(A_a)^2). \] Summing expectations and using gives \[ sum_a Vert (A_a-R_a)ot I ketpsiVert^2 leq frac2zetadelta, \] so A_a ot I approx_2zeta/delta R_a ot I. For every x in [0,1], one has trunc_delta(x) leq x/(1-delta), hence \[ R_a leq frac11-delta A_a. \] Summing over a and using that A is a measurement, \[ R = sum_a R_a leq frac11-delta I leq (1+2delta)I, \] where the last estimate uses delta leq 1/2. Setting delta=sqrtzeta gives the claim, and ensures delta leq 1/2. [Lean auxiliary declarations for rounding to projectors] The source-facing Lean declarations for Lemma~ are the proposition projectiveNonMeasurement and the construction theorem projectiveNonMeasurement\_of\_sourceAlmostProjective\_full. The declarations listed here are the endpoint and regime splits, the AlmostProjMeasStatement witness forms, and the spectral-truncation statement conversions used by later Section~5 arguments. They are not additional hypotheses in the paper statement of Lemma~. [Combinatorial averaging for the r > d branch] Let f : alpha to R be a function on a finite index set alpha with |alpha| = r, and let L subseteq alpha with |L| = d and d < r. Write S = L^complement and assume f(s) leq f(l) for every s in S and l in L. Then the pairwise double-counting inequality \[ |L|\, sum_s in S f(s) leq |S|\, sum_l in L f(l) \] holds, and hence also \[ r\, sum_s in S f(s) leq |S|\, sum_x in alpha f(x). \] If in addition r leq (1+2sqrtzeta)\,d, sum_x in alpha f(x) leq 1 + 2sqrtzeta, and 0 leq zeta leq 1/4, then \[ sum_s in S f(s) leq 4sqrtzeta. \] Choose L to be a set of d indices on which the sum of f is maximal. If some s in S and l in L satisfied f(l) < f(s), replacing l by s would increase this sum, so every small index is bounded by every large index. Summing the inequalities f(s) leq f(l) over all pairs (s,l) in S times L gives \[ |L|sum_s in S f(s) leq |S|sum_l in L f(l). \] Since alpha is the disjoint union of L and S, adding |S|sum_s in S f(s) to both sides yields \[ rsum_s in S f(s) leq |S|sum_x in alpha f(x). \] The hypotheses |L|=d and r leq (1+2sqrtzeta)d imply |S|/r leq 2sqrtzeta. Dividing by r and using sum_x in alpha f(x) leq 1+2sqrtzeta gives \[ sum_s in S f(s) leq 2sqrtzeta(1+2sqrtzeta). \] Finally, zeta leq 1/4 implies sqrtzeta leq 1/2, and hence 2sqrtzeta(1+2sqrtzeta) leq 4sqrtzeta. [Rank reduction] There exists a set of projection matrices \Q_a\ such that A_a ot I approx_12sqrtzeta Q_a ot I. and Q:= sum_a Q_a leq (1+2sqrtzeta) cdot I. Furthermore, sum_a rank(Q_a) leq d. Let \R_a\ be given by . Write r_a=rank(R_a) and r=sum_a r_a. If r leq d, take Q_a=R_a. Otherwise, r = sum_a r_a = sum_a Tr(R_a) = Tr(R) leq (1+2sqrtzeta)d. Let ketv_a,1,ldots,ketv_a,r_a be an orthonormal basis for the range of R_a, so \[ R_a = sum_i=1^r_a ketv_a,ibrav_a,i. \] Define the overlaps \[ o_a,i = brapsi (ketv_a,ibrav_a,i ot I)ketpsi. \] Their total satisfies sum_a sum_i=1^r_a o_a,i = brapsi R ot I ketpsi leq 1+2sqrtzeta. Let Large be the set of the d largest overlaps o_a,i, breaking ties arbitrarily, and let Small be the complement. Then |Small| = r-d leq 2sqrtzeta\,d leq 2sqrtzeta\,r, by . Averaging the overlaps over the r indices gives sum_(a,i)in Small o_a,i leq frac|Small|rsum_a,i o_a,i leq 4sqrtzeta, using , , and . For each a, let Large_a=\i : (a,i)in Large\ and define \[ Q_a = sum_i in Large_a ketv_a,ibrav_a,i. \] Then sum_a rank(Q_a)=|Large| leq d, and Q_a leq R_a for every a, so \[ Q = sum_a Q_a leq sum_a R_a = R leq (1+2sqrtzeta)I. \] Also, \[ R_a-Q_a = sum_i in Small_a ketv_a,ibrav_a,i \] is a projector, hence \[ sum_a Vert (R_a-Q_a)ot I ketpsiVert^2 = sum_(a,i)inSmall o_a,i leq 4sqrtzeta \] by . Therefore R_a ot I approx_4sqrtzeta Q_a ot I. Combining this with and the triangle inequality for approx_delta gives \[ A_a ot I approx_12sqrtzeta Q_a ot I. \] Henceforth let Q=\Q_a\ be the family given by . [Completeness of~Q] brapsi Q ot I ketpsi geq 1 - 11 zeta^1/4. Since each Q_a is projective, brapsi Q ot I ketpsi = sum_a brapsi (Q_a)^2 ot I ketpsi approx_5zeta^1/4 sum_a brapsi (Q_a cdot A_a)ot I ketpsi. By Cauchy--Schwarz, \[ sum_a brapsi (Q_a)^2 ot I ketpsi leq 1+2sqrtzeta quadand sum_a brapsi (Q_a-A_a)^2 ot I ketpsi leq 12sqrtzeta \] from . A second Cauchy--Schwarz estimate yields sum_a brapsi (Q_a cdot A_a)ot I ketpsi approx_4zeta^1/4 sum_a brapsi (A_a)^2 ot I ketpsi. Combining and with gives \[ brapsi Q ot I ketpsi geq sum_a brapsi A_a ot I ketpsi - 2zeta - 9zeta^1/4 = 1 - 11zeta^1/4, \] since zeta leq zeta^1/4 under . [Completeness of~sqrtQ] brapsi sqrtQ ot I ketpsi geq 1 - 12 zeta^1/4. Diagonalize Q=sum_i nu_i ketu_ibrau_i. Because Q leq (1+2sqrtzeta)I by , each nu_i is at most 1+2sqrtzeta. Therefore \[ sqrtQ = sum_i sqrtnu_iketu_ibrau_i geq frac1sqrt1+2sqrtzeta Q. \] The scalar estimate \[ frac1sqrt1+2sqrtzeta geq 1-sqrtzeta \] gives sqrtQ geq (1-sqrtzeta)Q. Hence implies \[ brapsi sqrtQ ot I ketpsi geq (1-sqrtzeta)(1-11zeta^1/4) geq 1-12zeta^1/4. \] [Q is almost projective] sum_a (Q_a cdot Q cdot Q_a - Q_a) leq 4sqrtzeta cdot I. Since Q leq (1+2sqrtzeta)I by , sum_a Q_a cdot Q cdot Q_a - sum_a Q_a & leq (1+2sqrtzeta) sum_a Q_a cdot I cdot Q_a - sum_a Q_a \\ & = (1+2sqrtzeta)Q - Q \\ & = 2sqrtzeta\,Q \\ & leq 2sqrtzeta(1+2sqrtzeta)I \\ & leq 4sqrtzeta\,I, using in the last step. [Matrix decomposition of~Q_a] For each a, let \[ m_a = rank(Q_a), \] and let ketv_a,1,ldots,ketv_a,m_a be an orthonormal basis for the range of Q_a, so that \[ Q_a = sum_i=1^m_a ketv_a,ibrav_a,i. \] Let \[ m = sum_a m_a, \] and let \keta,i\ be an orthonormal basis of C^m, indexed by all a and all 1 leq i leq m_a. For each a, define \[ X_a = sum_i=1^m_a keta,ibrav_a,i, T_a = sum_i=1^m_a keta,ibraa,i, \] and define X = sum_a X_a = sum_a sum_i=1^m_a keta,ibrav_a,i. Let T = \T_a\. Then T is a projective measurement on C^m. Choose an orthonormal basis of the range of each projector \(Q_a\). The rank-one expansion gives the displayed decomposition, and the orthogonality of the labelled basis vectors makes the family \(T\) a projective measurement. [SVD of~X] The paper presents this step by choosing a singular value decomposition \[ X = U cdot Sigma_m times d cdot V^dagger. \] The formalization has two closely related auxiliary declarations. The reduced datum records the downstream consequences of the choice: the matrices X and widehat X, the identities X^dagger X=Q, widehat Xwidehat X^dagger=I, and X^daggerwidehat X=sqrt Q, together with the Q_a=X^dagger T_aX restatement. The rectangular-SVD lemmas take explicit matrices U,V,Sigma,I_mtimes d and derive the two stored widehat X identities from the matrix calculation below. Apply the finite-dimensional singular value decomposition to \(X\) and record exactly the consequences used later: the identities for \(X^dagger X\), \(widehat Xwidehat X^dagger\), \(X^daggerwidehat X\), and the restatement of the \(Q_a\)'s. The unitary-group constructors are the same rectangular-SVD calculation, with the square factors taken as elements of the relevant unitary groups rather than as matrices accompanied by separate unitarity equations. In the sigma-range specialization, the auxiliary row space is the lifted finite-enumeration carrier associated to the ranks of the \(Q_a\)'s, which is definitionally the carrier of the canonical sigma-range \(Q\)-layer. [Formalization support for orthogonal projector families] If the family \Q_a\ were a projective measurement, then the vectors ketv_a,i, over all a and all 1 leq i leq m_a, would be orthonormal. Then would already be a singular value decomposition of X, with Sigma = I_m times d. Equivalently, \[ X = U cdot I_m times d cdot V^dagger. \] This motivates replacing Sigma by I in the definition of widehat X and P. [Definition of~P] The paper defines \[ widehatX = U cdot I_m times d cdot V^dagger. \] We take widehat X to be the reduced matrix supplied by the stored datum. For each a, define \[ widehatX_a = T_a cdot widehatX, P_a = widehatX_a^dagger cdot widehatX_a. \] The definition is the formal \(Q/X/widehat X/P\) construction: once \(widehat X\) is chosen from the stored singular-value data, each \(P_a\) is defined as the positive operator \(widehat X_a^daggerwidehat X_a\). For each a, \[ X_a = T_a cdot X. \] Multiply the definition of X by T_a on the left and use that T_a selects exactly the basis vectors keta,i: \[ T_a cdot X = Big(sum_i=1^m_a keta,ibraa,iBig) Big(sum_b sum_j=1^m_b ketb,jbrav_b,jBig) = sum_i=1^m_a keta,ibrav_a,i = X_a. \] [Q_a restated] For each a, Q_a = X_a^dagger cdot X_a = X^dagger cdot T_a cdot X = X_a^dagger cdot X. The identity X_a^dagger X_a = Q_a follows by expanding the basis sums. 	\begin{lemma}\label{lem:trunc-inequality}
		
		
		For any $x \in [0, 1]$,
		\begin{equation*}
			(x - \mathsf{trunc}_\delta(x))^2 \leq \frac{1}{\delta} \cdot (x - x^2).
		\end{equation*}
	\end{lemma}
	\begin{proof}

		\]

	\end{proof}

	\end{lemma}

	\begin{lemma}[Combinatorial averaging for the $r > d$ branch]\label{lem:small-overlap-averaging}
		
		
		
		
		
		Let $f : \alpha \to \mathbb{R}$ be a function on a finite index set $\alpha$ with
		$|\alpha| = r$, and let $L \subseteq \alpha$ with $|L| = d$ and $d < r$. Write
		$S = L^\complement$ and assume $f(s) \leq f(l)$ for every $s \in S$ and $l \in L$.
		Then the pairwise double-counting inequality
		\[
			|L|\, \sum_{s \in S} f(s) \leq |S|\, \sum_{l \in L} f(l)
		\]
		holds, and hence also
		\[
			r\, \sum_{s \in S} f(s) \leq |S|\, \sum_{x \in \alpha} f(x).
		\]
		If in addition $r \leq (1+2\sqrt{\zeta})\,d$, $\sum_{x \in \alpha} f(x) \leq
		1 + 2\sqrt{\zeta}$, and $0 \leq \zeta \leq 1/4$, then
		\[
			\sum_{s \in S} f(s) \leq 4\sqrt{\zeta}.
		\]
	\end{lemma}
	\begin{proof}
		
		Choose $L$ to be a set of $d$ indices on which the sum of $f$ is maximal. If some $s \in S$ and $l \in L$ satisfied $f(l) < f(s)$, replacing $l$ by $s$ would increase this sum, so every small index is bounded by every large index. Summing the inequalities $f(s) \leq f(l)$ over all pairs $(s,l) \in S \times L$ gives
		\[
			|L|\sum_{s \in S} f(s) \leq |S|\sum_{l \in L} f(l).
		\]
		Since $\alpha$ is the disjoint union of $L$ and $S$, adding $|S|\sum_{s \in S} f(s)$ to both sides yields
		\[
			r\sum_{s \in S} f(s) \leq |S|\sum_{x \in \alpha} f(x).
		\]
		The hypotheses $|L|=d$ and $r \leq (1+2\sqrt{\zeta})d$ imply $|S|/r \leq 2\sqrt{\zeta}$. Dividing by $r$ and using $\sum_{x \in \alpha} f(x) \leq 1+2\sqrt{\zeta}$ gives
		\[
			\sum_{s \in S} f(s) \leq 2\sqrt{\zeta}(1+2\sqrt{\zeta}).
		\]
		Finally, $\zeta \leq 1/4$ implies $\sqrt{\zeta} \leq 1/2$, and hence $2\sqrt{\zeta}(1+2\sqrt{\zeta}) \leq 4\sqrt{\zeta}$.
	\end{proof}

		and let $\ket{v_{a,1}},\ldots,\ket{v_{a,m_a}}$ be an orthonormal basis for the range of $Q_a$, so that
		\[
			Q_a = \sum_{i=1}^{m_a} \ket{v_{a,i}}\bra{v_{a,i}}.
		\]
		Let
		\[
			m = \sum_a m_a,
		\]
		and let $\{\ket{a,i}\}$ be an orthonormal basis of $\C^m$, indexed by all $a$ and all
		$1 \leq i \leq m_a$. For each $a$, define
		\[
			X_a = \sum_{i=1}^{m_a} \ket{a,i}\bra{v_{a,i}},
			\qquad
			T_a = \sum_{i=1}^{m_a} \ket{a,i}\bra{a,i},
		\]
		and define
		\begin{equation}\label{eq:looks-like-singular-value-decomposition}
			X = \sum_a X_a = \sum_a \sum_{i=1}^{m_a} \ket{a,i}\bra{v_{a,i}}.
		\end{equation}
		Let $T = \{T_a\}$. Then $T$ is a projective measurement on $\C^m$.
	\end{definition}
	\begin{proof}
		
		
		
		Choose an orthonormal basis of the range of each projector \(Q_a\).
		The rank-one expansion gives the displayed decomposition, and the
		orthogonality of the labelled basis vectors makes the family \(T\)
		a projective measurement.
	\end{proof}

	\begin{definition}[SVD of~$X$]\label{def:svd-of-X}
		
		
		
		
		
		
		
		
		
		
		
		
		
		
		
		
		
		
		
		
		
		
		
		
		
		
		
		The paper presents this step by choosing a singular value decomposition
		\[
			X = U \cdot \Sigma_{m \times d} \cdot V^\dagger.
		\]
		The formalization has two closely related auxiliary declarations.  The reduced
		datum records the downstream consequences of the choice: the matrices $X$
		and $\widehat X$, the identities $X^\dagger X=Q$,
		$\widehat X\widehat X^\dagger=I$, and $X^\dagger\widehat X=\sqrt Q$,
		together with the $Q_a=X^\dagger T_aX$ restatement.  The rectangular-SVD
		lemmas take explicit matrices $U,V,\Sigma,I_{m\times d}$ and derive the
		two stored $\widehat X$ identities from the matrix calculation below.
	\end{definition}
	\begin{proof}
		
		
		
		Apply the finite-dimensional singular value decomposition to \(X\) and
		record exactly the consequences used later: the identities for
		\(X^\dagger X\), \(\widehat X\widehat X^\dagger\),
		\(X^\dagger\widehat X\), and the restatement of the \(Q_a\)'s.  The
		unitary-group constructors are the same rectangular-SVD calculation, with
		the square factors taken as elements of the relevant unitary groups
		rather than as matrices accompanied by separate unitarity equations.  In
		the sigma-range specialization, the auxiliary row space is the lifted
		finite-enumeration carrier associated to the ranks of the \(Q_a\)'s, which
		is definitionally the carrier of the canonical sigma-range \(Q\)-layer.
	\end{proof}

	\begin{remark}[Formalization support for orthogonal projector families]\label{rem:motivation-for-P}
		If the family $\{Q_a\}$ were a projective measurement, then the vectors
		$\ket{v_{a,i}}$, over all $a$ and all $1 \leq i \leq m_a$, would be orthonormal.
		Then \eqref{eq:looks-like-singular-value-decomposition} would already be a singular value
		decomposition of $X$, with $\Sigma = I_{m \times d}$. Equivalently,
		\[
			X = U \cdot I_{m \times d} \cdot V^\dagger.
		\]
		This motivates replacing $\Sigma$ by $I$ in the definition of $\widehat X$ and $P$.
	\end{remark}

	\begin{definition}[Definition of~$P$]\label{def:projective-P}
		
		
		
		The paper defines
		\[
			\widehat{X} = U \cdot I_{m \times d} \cdot V^\dagger.
		\]
		We take $\widehat X$ to be the reduced matrix supplied by the stored datum.
		For each $a$, define
		\[
			\widehat{X}_a = T_a \cdot \widehat{X},
			\qquad
			P_a = \widehat{X}_a^\dagger \cdot \widehat{X}_a.
		\]
	\end{definition}
	\begin{proof}
		
		
		
		The definition is the formal \(Q/X/\widehat X/P\) construction: once
		\(\widehat X\) is chosen from the stored singular-value data, each
		\(P_a\) is defined as the positive operator
		\(\widehat X_a^\dagger\widehat X_a\).
	\end{proof}

	\begin{lemma}\label{lem:xa-t}
		
		
		
		For each $a$,
		\[
			X_a = T_a \cdot X.
		\]
	\end{lemma}
	\begin{proof}
		
		Multiply the definition of $X$ by $T_a$ on the left and use that $T_a$ selects exactly the basis vectors $\ket{a,i}$:
		\[
			T_a \cdot X
			=
			\Big(\sum_{i=1}^{m_a} \ket{a,i}\bra{a,i}\Big)
			\Big(\sum_b \sum_{j=1}^{m_b} \ket{b,j}\bra{v_{b,j}}\Big)
			=
			\sum_{i=1}^{m_a} \ket{a,i}\bra{v_{a,i}}
			=
			X_a.
		\]
	\end{proof}

	\begin{lemma}[$Q_a$ restated]\label{lem:qa-restated}
		
		
		For each $a$,
		\begin{equation*}
			Q_a = X_a^\dagger \cdot X_a = X^\dagger \cdot T_a \cdot X = X_a^\dagger \cdot X.
		\end{equation*}
	\end{lemma}
	\begin{proof}
		
		
		The identity $X_a^\dagger X_a = Q_a$ follows by expanding the basis sums. The remaining equalities come from \ref{lem:xa-t} and the projectivity of $T$:
		\[
			X_a^\dagger \cdot X_a
			=
			(X^\dagger \cdot T_a)(T_a \cdot X)
			=
			X^\dagger \cdot T_a \cdot X
			=
			X_a^\dagger \cdot X.
		\]
	\end{proof}

	\begin{lemma}[$X$ squared]\label{lem:X-squared}
		
		
		
		
		
		
		
		
		
		
		\begin{equation*}
			X^\dagger \cdot X = Q.
		\end{equation*}
	\end{lemma}
	\begin{proof}
		
		
		Use that $T$ is a measurement and then \ref{lem:qa-restated}:
		\[
			X^\dagger \cdot X
			=
			\sum_a X^\dagger \cdot T_a \cdot X
			=
			\sum_a Q_a
			=
			Q.
		\]
		The additional paper identities involving $U,V,\Sigma$ are the usual SVD
		computations.  The Lean development also records the spectral calculation
		which will identify the mixed positive-Gram-image product with
		$\sqrt Q$: the positive eigenvalues give the nonzero columns, while the
		zero eigenspace has zero coefficient in the square-root expansion and is
		killed by $X$.  The conjugate right-eigenvector rows over the positive
		spectrum are also orthonormal.  Equivalently, any row-space vector
		orthogonal to the positive Gram images is killed by $X^\dagger$.
	\end{proof}

	\begin{lemma}\label{lem:X-expression-to-Q-expression}
		
		
		For each $a$,
		\begin{equation*}
			X_a^\dagger \cdot (X \cdot X^\dagger - I_{m \times m})^2 \cdot X_a
			=
			Q_a \cdot Q \cdot Q_a - Q_a.
		\end{equation*}
	\end{lemma}
	\begin{proof}
		
		
		Expand the square and apply \ref{lem:X-squared} and \ref{lem:qa-restated} term by term:
		\[
			X_a^\dagger (X \cdot X^\dagger \cdot X \cdot X^\dagger) X_a
			=
			Q_a \cdot Q \cdot Q_a,
		\]
		while
		\[
			X_a^\dagger (X \cdot X^\dagger) X_a
			=
			(X_a^\dagger \cdot X)(X^\dagger \cdot X_a)
			=
			Q_a \cdot Q_a
			=
			Q_a,
		\]
		and $X_a^\dagger I_{m \times m} X_a = X_a^\dagger X_a = Q_a$. Substituting these identities into
		\[
			(X \cdot X^\dagger - I_{m \times m})^2
			=
			X \cdot X^\dagger \cdot X \cdot X^\dagger - 2X \cdot X^\dagger + I_{m \times m}
		\]
		gives the claim.
	\end{proof}

	\begin{lemma}[$P_a$ restated]\label{lem:pa-restated}
		
		
		For each $a$,
		\begin{equation*}
			P_a = \widehat{X}^\dagger \cdot T_a \cdot \widehat{X} = \widehat{X}_a^\dagger \cdot \widehat{X}.
		\end{equation*}
	\end{lemma}
	\begin{proof}
		
		
		Since $T$ is projective,
		\[
			P_a
			=
			\widehat{X}_a^\dagger \cdot \widehat{X}_a
			=
			(\widehat{X}^\dagger \cdot T_a)(T_a \cdot \widehat{X})
			=
			\widehat{X}^\dagger \cdot T_a \cdot \widehat{X}
			=
			\widehat{X}_a^\dagger \cdot \widehat{X}.
		\]
	\end{proof}

	\begin{lemma}[$\widehat{X}$ squared]\label{lem:X-hat-squared}
		
		
		
		
		
		
		
		
		
		
		
		
		
		
		
		
		
		
		
		
		
		
		
		
		
		
		
		
		
		
		
		\begin{equation*}
			\widehat{X} \cdot \widehat{X}^\dagger = I_{m \times m}.
		\end{equation*}
	\end{lemma}
	\begin{proof}
		
		The paper proves this by multiplying out
		$\widehat{X}=U\cdot I_{m\times d}\cdot V^\dagger$ and using the unitarity of
		$U$ and $V$.  In Lean, the dimension hypothesis $m\leq d$ already gives a
		rectangular matrix with orthonormal rows on the sigma auxiliary space; the
		chosen matrix \texttt{sigmaFinXHatCoisometry} and its specification record this
		existence result as a hypothesis for the future construction.  The formal lemma
		\texttt{orthonormal\_normalized\_image\_of\_adjoint\_comp\_eigenvectors}
		records the singular-vector normalization calculation, while
		\texttt{normalized\_matrix\_image\_rows\_mul\_conjTranspose} combines the
		corresponding row-coisometry identity, and
		\texttt{positive\_gram\_spectrum\_image\_rows\_transpose\_mixed} records the
		adjoint action $X^\dagger(\lambda^{-1/2}Xv)=\lambda^{1/2}v$ on the positive
		spectral part of the Gram operator.  The formal lemma
		\texttt{exists\_unitaryGroup\_with\_positive\_gram\_spectrum\_rows} records the
		next finite-dimensional step: after choosing distinct row positions for the
		positive spectrum, these normalized image rows extend to a square unitary
		group element on the row space.  The companion lemma
		\texttt{exists\_rectangular\_coisometry\_extending\_orthonormal\_rows}
		records the analogous rectangular completion for prescribed right rows
		when the dimension bound permits it.  The formal lemma
		\texttt{unitaryGroup\_mul\_rectangular\_coisometry} and its right-multiplication
		companion
		\texttt{rectangular\_coisometry\_mul\_conjTranspose\_unitaryGroup} record the
		two unitary-preservation steps in the paper's multiplication.  The formal
		lemma \texttt{rectangularSvd\_xHat\_coisometry\_unitaryGroup} applies these
		preservation steps to the rectangular-SVD expression.  The
		unconditional positive-Gram route is
		\texttt{exists\_xHat\_of\_sigmaFinRangeEmbedding\_positiveGram}, which
		constructs $\widehat X$ from the rank-reduction witness and proves
		$\widehat X\widehat X^\dagger=I$ together with the mixed square-root
		identity below.
	\end{proof}

	\begin{lemma}[$X$ times $\widehat{X}$]\label{lem:X-times-X-hat}
		
		
		
		
		
		
		
		
		
		
		
		
		
		
		
		
		
		
		
		\begin{equation*}
			X \cdot \widehat{X}^\dagger =
			U \cdot \Sigma_{m \times m} \cdot U^\dagger,
			\quad
			X^\dagger \cdot \widehat{X} = \sqrt{Q}.
		\end{equation*}
	\end{lemma}
	\begin{proof}
		
		
		The paper obtains this from the SVD formula for $X$ and the definition of
		$\widehat X$.  In Lean, the unconditional QXP data first proves that
		$X\widehat X^\dagger$ is Hermitian and positive.  The formal lemma
		\texttt{x\_mul\_xHat\_adjoint\_spectral\_theorem} then applies Mathlib's
		spectral theorem for Hermitian matrices, giving the displayed
		$U\Sigma U^\dagger$ form with the Mathlib eigenvector unitary and the
		diagonal matrix of real eigenvalues.  The auxiliary lemma
		\texttt{rectangularSvd\_x\_mul\_xHat\_conjTranspose\_raw} records the same
		calculation under explicit rectangular-SVD data, where the middle factor
		\(S I_{m\times d}^\dagger\) is the formal square matrix
		\(\Sigma_{m\times m}\).  The formal lemma
		\texttt{rectangularSvd\_xHat\_mixed\_of\_sqrtQ\_unitaryGroup} records the
		second matrix calculation in the form whose square-root target is the
		operator $Q$ supplied by the QXP construction.  The formal lemma
		\texttt{rectangularSvd\_middle\_eq\_sqrt\_of\_square} records the spectral
		step: a positive middle factor whose square is $Q$ is the positive square
		root of $Q$.  The reduced datum then records this mixed-product
		identity as a primitive consequence, which is exactly the part needed in
		\ref{lem:squared-difference} and \ref{lem:P-Q-approx}.
	\end{proof}

	\begin{remark}[Lean status for the QXP algebra]\label{rem:qxp-layer-lean-status}
		The Lean declarations linked in Lemmas~\ref{lem:X-squared},
		\ref{lem:X-hat-squared}, and~\ref{lem:X-times-X-hat} expose the
		corresponding matrix identities as construction theorems.  These
		declarations prove the identities from the \(Q\)-layer, the sigma-range
		realization, and the positive-Gram spectral construction, with the
		rectangular-SVD calculation retained as an auxiliary comparison.  Thus the
		local \(X/\widehat X/P\) algebra is formalized; the remaining chapter-level
		work is to compose this construction with the preceding orthonormalization
		step from the paper hypotheses.
	\end{remark}

	\begin{lemma}[Squared difference]\label{lem:squared-difference}
		
		
		
		
		
		
		\begin{equation*}
			(X - \widehat{X}) \cdot (X - \widehat{X})^\dagger \leq (X \cdot X^\dagger - I_{m \times m})^2.
		\end{equation*}
	\end{lemma}
	\begin{proof}
		
		
		The paper diagonalizes the positive operator $X\widehat X^\dagger$ using the
		SVD notation.  The formal proof avoids storing that SVD explicitly: set
		$Y=X\widehat X^\dagger$.  The primitive identities imply that $Y$ is
		hermitian, nonnegative, and satisfies $Y^2=XX^\dagger$.  Hence
		$(X-\widehat X)(X-\widehat X)^\dagger=(Y-I)^2$, and positivity of $Y$ gives
		$(Y-I)^2\leq(Y^2-I)^2=(XX^\dagger-I)^2$.
	\end{proof}

	\begin{lemma}[Projectivity of~$P$]\label{lem:P-projectivity}
		
		
		
		
		
		
		
		
		$P = \{P_a\}$ forms a projective sub-measurement.
	\end{lemma}
	\begin{proof}
		
		
		For outcomes $a,b$,
		\begin{align*}
			P_a \cdot P_b
			 & =
			(\widehat{X}^\dagger \cdot T_a \cdot \widehat{X})
			(\widehat{X}^\dagger \cdot T_b \cdot \widehat{X})                              \\
			 & =
			\widehat{X}^\dagger \cdot T_a \cdot I_{m \times m} \cdot T_b \cdot \widehat{X} \\
			 & =
			\widehat{X}^\dagger \cdot T_a \cdot \widehat{X} \cdot \bone[a=b]               \\
			 & =
			P_a \cdot \bone[a=b],
		\end{align*}
		where the second line uses \ref{lem:X-hat-squared}, the third uses that $T$ is projective, and the last uses \ref{lem:pa-restated}. Summing over $a$ shows $\sum_a P_a \leq I$, so $P$ is a projective sub-measurement.  The formalization also records the sharper identity
		\[
			\sum_a P_a=\widehat X^\dagger\widehat X,
		\]
		and the resulting total-domination estimates used later in the monotone-total self-improvement route.
	\end{proof}

	\begin{lemma}[$P$ is close to~$Q$]\label{lem:P-Q-approx}
		
		
		
		
		
		
		
		\begin{equation*}
			Q_a \ot I \approx_{30\zeta^{1/4}} P_a \ot I.
		\end{equation*}
	\end{lemma}
	\begin{proof}
		
		
		The formal proof follows this argument directly from the primitive
		$X$, $\widehat X$, and $P$ identities; the $30\zeta^{1/4}$ estimate is
		derived here rather than stored as part of the reduced datum.  The
		unitary-group rectangular-SVD lemma combines the same estimate with the
		positive-square identification of the middle factor from
		\ref{lem:X-times-X-hat}; the square unitary factors are again carried as
		elements of the relevant unitary groups.  The
		positive-Gram sigma-space lemma also records the coisometry
		\(X X^\dagger=I\) for the original sigma embedding when the projective
		\(Q\)-family is subnormalized; this is the construction-level hypothesis
		later used to obtain the QXP-internal fresh-outcome comparison
		\(Q_{\mathrm{none}} \leq P_{\mathrm{none}}\).  An additional
		source-to-\(Q\) comparison is still needed for source-facing residual
		domination.
		The quantity to bound is
		\begin{equation}\label{eq:P-Q-thing-to-bound}
			\sum_a \bra{\psi} (Q_a-P_a)^2 \ot I \ket{\psi}
			=
			\bra{\psi} Q \ot I \ket{\psi}
			+
			\bra{\psi} P \ot I \ket{\psi}
			-
			\sum_a \bra{\psi} Q_aP_a \ot I \ket{\psi}
			-
			\sum_a \bra{\psi} P_aQ_a \ot I \ket{\psi},
		\end{equation}
		using the projectivity of $Q$ and $P$. The first term is at most $1+2\sqrt{\zeta}$ by \ref{lem:projective-low-rank-sum}, and the second is at most $1$ because $P$ is a sub-measurement.

		For the last two terms,
		\begin{equation}\label{eq:complex-conjugates}
			\sum_a \bra{\psi} Q_aP_a \ot I \ket{\psi}
			+
			\sum_a \bra{\psi} P_aQ_a \ot I \ket{\psi}
			=
			2 \cdot \mathfrak{R}\Big(\sum_a \bra{\psi} Q_aP_a \ot I \ket{\psi}\Big).
		\end{equation}
		By \ref{lem:qa-restated},
		\[
			\sum_a \bra{\psi} Q_aP_a \ot I \ket{\psi}
			=
			\sum_a \bra{\psi} (X_a^\dagger \cdot X \cdot P_a) \ot I \ket{\psi}.
		\]
		The main estimate is
		\begin{equation}\label{eq:add-a-hat}
			\sum_a \bra{\psi} (X_a^\dagger \cdot X \cdot P_a)\ot I \ket{\psi}
			\approx_{2\zeta^{1/4}}
			\sum_a \bra{\psi} (X_a^\dagger \cdot \widehat{X} \cdot P_a)\ot I \ket{\psi}.
		\end{equation}
		This follows by Cauchy--Schwarz:
		\[
			\Big|\sum_a \bra{\psi} ((X_a^\dagger \cdot (X-\widehat X)) \ot I)\cdot(P_a \ot I)\ket{\psi}\Big|
		\]
		is bounded by the square root of
		\[
			\sum_a \bra{\psi} \big(X_a^\dagger \cdot (X-\widehat X)(X-\widehat X)^\dagger \cdot X_a\big)\ot I \ket{\psi},
		\]
		times the square root of $\sum_a \bra{\psi}(P_a)^2 \ot I \ket{\psi} \leq 1$. The first factor is at most $4\sqrt{\zeta}$ by \ref{lem:squared-difference}, \ref{lem:X-expression-to-Q-expression}, and \ref{lem:q-almost-projective}, so the total error is at most $2\zeta^{1/4}$.

		The right-hand side of \ref{eq:add-a-hat} is real, because
		\[
			\sum_a \bra{\psi} (X_a^\dagger \cdot \widehat{X} \cdot P_a)\ot I \ket{\psi}
			=
			\bra{\psi} (X^\dagger \cdot \widehat{X}) \ot I \ket{\psi}
			=
			\bra{\psi} \sqrt{Q} \ot I \ket{\psi},
		\]
		where the first equality uses \ref{lem:xa-t}, \ref{lem:pa-restated}, and \ref{lem:X-hat-squared} and that $T$ is a measurement, and the second uses \ref{lem:X-times-X-hat}. Hence \ref{lem:sqrt-Q-completeness} and \ref{eq:add-a-hat} imply
		\[
			\mathfrak{R}\Big(\sum_a \bra{\psi} Q_aP_a \ot I \ket{\psi}\Big)
			\geq
			1-14\zeta^{1/4}.
		\]
		Substituting this into \ref{eq:complex-conjugates} and then into \ref{eq:P-Q-thing-to-bound} gives
		\[
			\sum_a \bra{\psi} (Q_a-P_a)^2 \ot I \ket{\psi}
			\leq
			(1+2\sqrt{\zeta}) + 1 - 2(1-14\zeta^{1/4})
			=
			2\sqrt{\zeta} + 28\zeta^{1/4}
			\leq
			30\zeta^{1/4}.
		\]
	\end{proof}

	Finally, \ref{lem:projective-low-rank-sum} gives
	\[
		A_a \ot I \approx_{12\sqrt{\zeta}} Q_a \ot I,
	\]
	and \ref{lem:P-Q-approx} gives
	\[
		Q_a \ot I \approx_{30\zeta^{1/4}} P_a \ot I.
	\]
	The triangle inequality for $\approx_\delta$ yields
	\[
		A_a \ot I \approx_{84\zeta^{1/4}} P_a \ot I.
	\]

\label{lem:small-overlap-averaging}
		
		
		
		
		
		Let $f : \alpha \to \mathbb{R}$ be a function on a finite index set $\alpha$ with
		$|\alpha| = r$, and let $L \subseteq \alpha$ with $|L| = d$ and $d < r$. Write
		$S = L^\complement$ and assume $f(s) \leq f(l)$ for every $s \in S$ and $l \in L$.
		Then the pairwise double-counting inequality
		\[
			|L|\, \sum_{s \in S} f(s) \leq |S|\, \sum_{l \in L} f(l)
		\]
		holds, and hence also
		\[
			r\, \sum_{s \in S} f(s) \leq |S|\, \sum_{x \in \alpha} f(x).
		\]
		If in addition $r \leq (1+2\sqrt{\zeta})\,d$, $\sum_{x \in \alpha} f(x) \leq
		1 + 2\sqrt{\zeta}$, and $0 \leq \zeta \leq 1/4$, then
		\[
			\sum_{s \in S} f(s) \leq 4\sqrt{\zeta}.
		\]

Let $\{R_a\}$ be given by \ref{lem:projective-non-measurement}. Write $r_a=\mathrm{rank}(R_a)$ and $r=\sum_a r_a$. If $r \leq d$, take $Q_a=R_a$. Otherwise,
		\begin{equation}\label{eq:bound-on-r}
			r
			=
			\sum_a r_a
			=
			\sum_a \Tr(R_a)
			=
			\Tr(R)
			\leq
			(1+2\sqrt{\zeta})d.
		\end{equation}
		Let $\ket{v_{a,1}},\ldots,\ket{v_{a,r_a}}$ be an orthonormal basis for the range of $R_a$, so
		\[
			R_a = \sum_{i=1}^{r_a} \ket{v_{a,i}}\bra{v_{a,i}}.
		\]
		Define the overlaps
		\[
			o_{a,i} = \bra{\psi} (\ket{v_{a,i}}\bra{v_{a,i}} \ot I)\ket{\psi}.
		\]
		Their total satisfies
		\begin{equation}\label{eq:total-overlap}
			\sum_a \sum_{i=1}^{r_a} o_{a,i}
			=
			\bra{\psi} R \ot I \ket{\psi}
			\leq
			1+2\sqrt{\zeta}.
		\end{equation}
		Let $\mathsf{Large}$ be the set of the $d$ largest overlaps $o_{a,i}$, breaking ties arbitrarily, and let $\mathsf{Small}$ be the complement. Then
		\begin{equation}\label{eq:size-of-small-is-small}
			|\mathsf{Small}|
			=
			r-d
			\leq
			2\sqrt{\zeta}\,d
			\leq
			2\sqrt{\zeta}\,r,
		\end{equation}
		by \ref{eq:bound-on-r}. Averaging the overlaps over the $r$ indices gives
		\begin{equation}\label{eq:small-overlaps}
			\sum_{(a,i)\in \mathsf{Small}} o_{a,i}
			\leq
			\frac{|\mathsf{Small}|}{r}\sum_{a,i} o_{a,i}
			\leq
			4\sqrt{\zeta},
		\end{equation}
		using \ref{eq:size-of-small-is-small}, \ref{eq:total-overlap}, and \ref{eq:assumption-on-zeta}.

		\[
			Q_a = \sum_{i \in \mathsf{Large}_a} \ket{v_{a,i}}\bra{v_{a,i}}.
		\]

		\[
			Q = \sum_a Q_a \leq \sum_a R_a = R \leq (1+2\sqrt{\zeta})I.
		\]

nodes.statement: Diagonalize Q=sum_i nu_i ketu_ibrau_i. Because Q leq (1+2sqrtzeta)I by , each nu_i is at most 1+2sqrtzeta. Therefore \[ sqrtQ = sum_i sqrtnu_iketu_ibrau_i geq frac1sqrt1+2sqrtzeta Q. \] The scalar estimate \[ frac1sqrt1+2sqrtzeta geq 1-sqrtzeta \] gives sqrtQ geq (1-sqrtzeta)Q. Hence implies \[ brapsi sqrtQ ot I ketpsi geq (1-sqrtzeta)(1-11zeta^1/4) geq 1-12zeta^1/4. \]
nodes.raw_latex:
Diagonalize $Q=\sum_i \nu_i \ket{u_i}\bra{u_i}$. Because $Q \leq (1+2\sqrt{\zeta})I$ by \ref{lem:projective-low-rank-sum}, each $\nu_i$ is at most $1+2\sqrt{\zeta}$. Therefore
		\[
			\sqrt{Q}
			=
			\sum_i \sqrt{\nu_i}\ket{u_i}\bra{u_i}
			\geq
			\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+2\sqrt{\zeta}}} Q.
		\]
		The scalar estimate
		\[
			\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+2\sqrt{\zeta}}} \geq 1-\sqrt{\zeta}
		\]
		gives $\sqrt{Q} \geq (1-\sqrt{\zeta})Q$. Hence \ref{lem:Q-completeness} implies
		\[
			\bra{\psi} \sqrt{Q} \ot I \ket{\psi}
			\geq
			(1-\sqrt{\zeta})(1-11\zeta^{1/4})
			\geq
			1-12\zeta^{1/4}.
		\]

nodes.name: Matrix decomposition of~$Q_a$
nodes.statement: For each a, let \[ m_a = rank(Q_a), \] and let ketv_a,1,ldots,ketv_a,m_a be an orthonormal basis for the range of Q_a, so that \[ Q_a = sum_i=1^m_a ketv_a,ibrav_a,i. \] Let \[ m = sum_a m_a, \] and let \keta,i\ be an orthonormal basis of C^m, indexed by all a and all 1 leq i leq m_a. For each a, define \[ X_a = sum_i=1^m_a keta,ibrav_a,i, T_a = sum_i=1^m_a keta,ibraa,i, \] and define X = sum_a X_a = sum_a sum_i=1^m_a keta,ibrav_a,i. Let T = \T_a\. Then T is a projective measurement on C^m.
nodes.raw_latex:
\label{def:matrix-decomposition-Q}
		
		
		
		
		
		For each $a$, let
		\[
			m_a = \mathrm{rank}(Q_a),
		\]
		and let $\ket{v_{a,1}},\ldots,\ket{v_{a,m_a}}$ be an orthonormal basis for the range of $Q_a$, so that
		\[
			Q_a = \sum_{i=1}^{m_a} \ket{v_{a,i}}\bra{v_{a,i}}.
		\]
		Let
		\[
			m = \sum_a m_a,
		\]
		and let $\{\ket{a,i}\}$ be an orthonormal basis of $\C^m$, indexed by all $a$ and all
		$1 \leq i \leq m_a$. For each $a$, define
		\[
			X_a = \sum_{i=1}^{m_a} \ket{a,i}\bra{v_{a,i}},
			\qquad
			T_a = \sum_{i=1}^{m_a} \ket{a,i}\bra{a,i},
		\]
		and define
		\begin{equation}\label{eq:looks-like-singular-value-decomposition}
			X = \sum_a X_a = \sum_a \sum_{i=1}^{m_a} \ket{a,i}\bra{v_{a,i}}.
		\end{equation}
		Let $T = \{T_a\}$. Then $T$ is a projective measurement on $\C^m$.

nodes.name: Formalization support for orthogonal projector families
nodes.statement: If the family \Q_a\ were a projective measurement, then the vectors ketv_a,i, over all a and all 1 leq i leq m_a, would be orthonormal. Then would already be a singular value decomposition of X, with Sigma = I_m times d. Equivalently, \[ X = U cdot I_m times d cdot V^dagger. \] This motivates replacing Sigma by I in the definition of widehat X and P.
nodes.raw_latex:
\label{rem:motivation-for-P}
		If the family $\{Q_a\}$ were a projective measurement, then the vectors
		$\ket{v_{a,i}}$, over all $a$ and all $1 \leq i \leq m_a$, would be orthonormal.
		Then \eqref{eq:looks-like-singular-value-decomposition} would already be a singular value
		decomposition of $X$, with $\Sigma = I_{m \times d}$. Equivalently,
		\[
			X = U \cdot I_{m \times d} \cdot V^\dagger.
		\]
		This motivates replacing $\Sigma$ by $I$ in the definition of $\widehat X$ and $P$.

The formal proof follows this argument directly from the primitive
		$X$, $\widehat X$, and $P$ identities; the $30\zeta^{1/4}$ estimate is
		derived here rather than stored as part of the reduced datum.  The
		unitary-group rectangular-SVD lemma combines the same estimate with the
		positive-square identification of the middle factor from
		\ref{lem:X-times-X-hat}; the square unitary factors are again carried as
		elements of the relevant unitary groups.  The
		positive-Gram sigma-space lemma also records the coisometry
		\(X X^\dagger=I\) for the original sigma embedding when the projective
		\(Q\)-family is subnormalized; this is the construction-level hypothesis
		later used to obtain the QXP-internal fresh-outcome comparison
		\(Q_{\mathrm{none}} \leq P_{\mathrm{none}}\).  An additional
		source-to-\(Q\) comparison is still needed for source-facing residual
		domination.
		The quantity to bound is
		\begin{equation}\label{eq:P-Q-thing-to-bound}
			\sum_a \bra{\psi} (Q_a-P_a)^2 \ot I \ket{\psi}
			=
			\bra{\psi} Q \ot I \ket{\psi}
			+
			\bra{\psi} P \ot I \ket{\psi}
			-
			\sum_a \bra{\psi} Q_aP_a \ot I \ket{\psi}
			-
			\sum_a \bra{\psi} P_aQ_a \ot I \ket{\psi},
		\end{equation}
		using the projectivity of $Q$ and $P$. The first term is at most $1+2\sqrt{\zeta}$ by \ref{lem:projective-low-rank-sum}, and the second is at most $1$ because $P$ is a sub-measurement.

		For the last two terms,
		\begin{equation}\label{eq:complex-conjugates}
			\sum_a \bra{\psi} Q_aP_a \ot I \ket{\psi}
			+
			\sum_a \bra{\psi} P_aQ_a \ot I \ket{\psi}
			=
			2 \cdot \mathfrak{R}\Big(\sum_a \bra{\psi} Q_aP_a \ot I \ket{\psi}\Big).
		\end{equation}
		By \ref{lem:qa-restated},
		\[
			\sum_a \bra{\psi} Q_aP_a \ot I \ket{\psi}
			=
			\sum_a \bra{\psi} (X_a^\dagger \cdot X \cdot P_a) \ot I \ket{\psi}.
		\]
		The main estimate is
		\begin{equation}\label{eq:add-a-hat}
			\sum_a \bra{\psi} (X_a^\dagger \cdot X \cdot P_a)\ot I \ket{\psi}
			\approx_{2\zeta^{1/4}}
			\sum_a \bra{\psi} (X_a^\dagger \cdot \widehat{X} \cdot P_a)\ot I \ket{\psi}.
		\end{equation}
		This follows by Cauchy--Schwarz:
		\[
			\Big|\sum_a \bra{\psi} ((X_a^\dagger \cdot (X-\widehat X)) \ot I)\cdot(P_a \ot I)\ket{\psi}\Big|
		\]
		is bounded by the square root of
		\[
			\sum_a \bra{\psi} \big(X_a^\dagger \cdot (X-\widehat X)(X-\widehat X)^\dagger \cdot X_a\big)\ot I \ket{\psi},
		\]
		times the square root of $\sum_a \bra{\psi}(P_a)^2 \ot I \ket{\psi} \leq 1$. The first factor is at most $4\sqrt{\zeta}$ by \ref{lem:squared-difference}, \ref{lem:X-expression-to-Q-expression}, and \ref{lem:q-almost-projective}, so the total error is at most $2\zeta^{1/4}$.

		The right-hand side of \ref{eq:add-a-hat} is real, because
		\[
			\sum_a \bra{\psi} (X_a^\dagger \cdot \widehat{X} \cdot P_a)\ot I \ket{\psi}
			=
			\bra{\psi} (X^\dagger \cdot \widehat{X}) \ot I \ket{\psi}
			=
			\bra{\psi} \sqrt{Q} \ot I \ket{\psi},
		\]
		where the first equality uses \ref{lem:xa-t}, \ref{lem:pa-restated}, and \ref{lem:X-hat-squared} and that $T$ is a measurement, and the second uses \ref{lem:X-times-X-hat}. Hence \ref{lem:sqrt-Q-completeness} and \ref{eq:add-a-hat} imply
		\[
			\mathfrak{R}\Big(\sum_a \bra{\psi} Q_aP_a \ot I \ket{\psi}\Big)
			\geq
			1-14\zeta^{1/4}.
		\]
		Substituting this into \ref{eq:complex-conjugates} and then into \ref{eq:P-Q-thing-to-bound} gives
		\[
			\sum_a \bra{\psi} (Q_a-P_a)^2 \ot I \ket{\psi}
			\leq
			(1+2\sqrt{\zeta}) + 1 - 2(1-14\zeta^{1/4})
			=
			2\sqrt{\zeta} + 28\zeta^{1/4}
			\leq
			30\zeta^{1/4}.
		\]

nodes.name: Rerandomizing one coordinate
nodes.statement: For u in F_q^m, an index i in \1,dots,m\, and x in F_q, let \[ rerand_i(u,x) = u + x e_i. \] This is the move obtained by rerandomizing the i-th coordinate of u by a uniform additive shift. In Lean, the same edge distribution is represented as the push-forward of the uniform distribution on triples (u,i,x) by the map that replaces the i-th coordinate by x; since x is uniform, this is the same distribution as the additive-shift presentation. The corresponding weight-sum identity identifies this push-forward distribution with the explicit edge coefficient used in the matrix proof.
nodes.raw_latex:
\label{def:rerandomize-coord}
	
	
	
	
	
	For $u \in \F_q^m$, an index $i \in \{1,\dots,m\}$, and $x \in \F_q$, let
	\[
		\operatorname{rerand}_i(u,x) = u + x e_i.
	\]
	This is the move obtained by rerandomizing the $i$-th coordinate of $u$ by a uniform additive shift.
	In Lean, the same edge distribution is represented as the push-forward of the uniform distribution
	on triples $(u,i,x)$ by the map that replaces the $i$-th coordinate by $x$; since $x$ is uniform,
	this is the same distribution as the additive-shift presentation.  The corresponding
	weight-sum identity identifies this push-forward distribution with the explicit edge
	coefficient used in the matrix proof.

nodes.name: Hypercube graph
nodes.statement: The hypercube graph C=(V,E) has vertex set V=F_q^m, and an edge between u and v whenever they differ in at most one coordinate. A random edge (u,v) sim C is sampled by drawing u sim F_q^m, i in \1,dots,m\, and x in F_q uniformly and then setting v=rerand_i(u,x).
nodes.raw_latex:
\label{def:hypercube-graph}
	
	
	
	The hypercube graph $C=(V,E)$ has vertex set $V=\F_q^m$, and an edge between $u$ and $v$ whenever they differ in at most one coordinate. A random edge $(u,v) \sim C$ is sampled by drawing $u \sim \F_q^m$, $i \in \{1,\dots,m\}$, and $x \in \F_q$ uniformly and then setting $v=\operatorname{rerand}_i(u,x)$.

nodes.name: Adjacency matrix and Laplacian
nodes.statement: Let M=q^m. The normalized adjacency matrix of C is \[ K = E_(u,v)sim C ketubrav, \] and the Laplacian is \[ L = frac1MI-K. \]
nodes.raw_latex:
\label{def:adjacency-laplacian}
	
	
	
	Let $M=q^m$. The normalized adjacency matrix of $C$ is
	\[
		K = \E_{(u,v)\sim C} \ket{u}\bra{v},
	\]
	and the Laplacian is
	\[
		L = \frac{1}{M}I-K.
	\]

We first compute
	\[
		A_0
		=
		(\bra{\varphi_0}\ot I)\cdot A_{\mathrm{comb}}
		=
		\left(\frac{1}{M^{1/2}} \cdot \sum_{u \in \F_q^m} \bra{u}\right) \ot I \cdot \left(\sum_{u \in \F_q^m} \ket{u} \ot A^u \ot I\right)
		=
		\frac{1}{M^{1/2}} \cdot \sum_{u \in \F_q^m} A^u \ot I.
	\]
	Writing $A_{\mathrm{avg}}=\E_u A^u$, it follows that
	\[
		\ket{\varphi_0}\ot A_0
		=
		\sum_{u \in \F_q^m} \ket{u} \ot A_{\mathrm{avg}} \ot I,
		\qquad
		\ket{\varphi_\perp}\ot A_\perp
		=
		\sum_{u \in \F_q^m} \ket{u} \ot (A^u-A_{\mathrm{avg}}) \ot I.
	\]
	Hence
	\begin{equation}
		\frac{1}{M} \cdot \Tr((\bra{\varphi_\perp}\ot A_\perp)(I\ot \ket{\psi}\bra{\psi})(\ket{\varphi_\perp}\ot A_\perp))
		=
		\E_{u \sim \F_q^m} \bra{\psi} (A^u-A_{\mathrm{avg}})^2 \ot I \ket{\psi}.
		\label{eq:just-took-trace}
	\end{equation}

	\[
		\E_{u \sim \F_q^m}(A^u-A_{\mathrm{avg}})^2
		=
		\E_{u \sim \F_q^m}\bigl((A^u)^2-(A_{\mathrm{avg}})^2\bigr)
		=
		\frac12 \E_{u,v \sim \F_q^m} (A^u-A^v)^2.
	\]

	\[
		\frac{1}{M} \cdot \Tr((\bra{\varphi_\perp}\ot A_\perp)(I\ot \ket{\psi}\bra{\psi})(\ket{\varphi_\perp}\ot A_\perp))
		=
		\frac12 \E_{u,v \sim \F_q^m} \bra{\psi} (A^u-A^v)^2 \ot I \ket{\psi}
		=
		\mathbf{Var}_{\mathrm{global}}(A,\psi).
	\]

We want to bound
	\begin{equation}
		\E_{u,v \sim \F_q^m} \sum_{g \in \polyfunc{m}{q}{d}} \lVert (A^u_{g(u)}-A^v_{g(v)}) \ot (G_g)^{1/2} \ket{\psi} \rVert^2
		=
		\E_{u,v \sim \F_q^m} \sum_{g \in \polyfunc{m}{q}{d}} \bra{\psi} (A^u_{g(u)}-A^v_{g(v)})^2 \ot G_g \ket{\psi}.
		\label{eq:global-variance-target}
	\end{equation}
	For each $g \in \polyfunc{m}{q}{d}$, define
	\[
		A(g)^u := A^u_{g(u)},
		\qquad
		\ket{\psi_g} := (I \ot (G_g)^{1/2})\ket{\psi}.
	\]
	Then
	\[
		\eqref{eq:global-variance-target}
		=
		\sum_{g \in \polyfunc{m}{q}{d}} \E_{u,v \sim \F_q^m} \bra{\psi_g} (A(g)^u-A(g)^v)^2 \ot I \ket{\psi_g}
		=
		\sum_{g \in \polyfunc{m}{q}{d}} 2\,\mathbf{Var}_{\mathrm{global}}(A(g),\psi_g).
	\]
	Applying Lemma~\ref{lem:local-to-global} gives
	\[
		\eqref{eq:global-variance-target}
		\le
		\sum_{g \in \polyfunc{m}{q}{d}} 2m\,\mathbf{Var}_{\mathrm{local}}(A(g),\psi_g)
		=
		m \cdot \sum_{g \in \polyfunc{m}{q}{d}} \E_{(u,v)\sim C} \bra{\psi} (A^u_{g(u)}-A^v_{g(v)})^2 \ot G_g \ket{\psi}.
	\]
	The last quantity is at most $m \cdot 24\left(\eps+\delta+\frac{md}{q}\right)$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:equivalent-local-variance}, which is exactly \ref{eq:global-variance-of-points-equation}.

\label{lem:self-improvement-helper}
  
  
  
  
  Let $G \in \polymeas{m}{q}{d}$ be a measurement with the following property:
  \begin{enumerate}
    \item (Consistency with~$A$): \label{item:self-improvement-G-consistency} On average over $u \sim \F_q^{m}$,
    \[
      A^{u}_a \ot I \simeq_{\nu} I \ot G_{[g(u)=a]}.
    \]
  \end{enumerate}
  Let
  \[
    \zeta = 100m\cdot \Big(\eps^{1/2} + \delta^{1/2} + (d/q)^{1/2}\Big).
  \]
  Then there exists $H \in \polysub{m}{q}{d}$ with the following properties:
  \begin{enumerate}
    \item (Completeness): \label{item:self-improvement-completeness} If $H = \sum_h H_h$, then
    \[
      \bra{\psi} H \ot I \ket{\psi} \geq (1-\nu)-\zeta.
    \]
    \item (Consistency with~$A$): \label{item:self-improvement-A-consistency} On average over $u \sim \F_q^m$,
    \[
      A^u_a \ot I \simeq_{\zeta} I \ot H_{[h(u) = a]}.
    \]
    \item (Strong self-consistency): \label{item:self-improvement-self}
    \[
      \sum_{h} \bra{\psi} H_h \ot H_h \ket{\psi} \geq \bra{\psi} H \ot I \ket{\psi} - \zeta.
    \]
    \item (Boundedness): \label{item:self-improvement-boundedness} There exists a positive-semidefinite matrix~$Z$ such that
    \[
      \bra{\psi} Z \ot I \ket{\psi} -\E_{u} \sum_a \bra{\psi}  A^{u}_{a} \ot H_{[h(u)=a]} \ket{\psi} \leq \zeta
    \]
    and for each $h \in \polyfunc{m}{q}{d}$,
    \[
      Z \geq \left(\E_{u} A^{u}_{h(u)}\right).
    \]
  \end{enumerate}

nodes.statement: Let T=\T_g\ and Z be the optimal solutions to the SDPs~ and~ given by Lemma~. Then T is a measurement, and forall g in polyfuncmqd: Z &geq left(E_u A^u_g(u)right), \\ T_g cdot Z &= T_g cdot left(E_u A^u_g(u)right). For each u in F_q^m, define H^u=\H_h^u\_h in polyfuncmqd by \[ H_h^u := A^u_h(u) cdot T_h cdot A^u_h(u), \] and let \[ H_h := E_u H_h^u. \] The pointwise family H^u is a submeasurement because \[ sum_h H_h^u = sum_a A_a^u cdot Big(sum_h:h(u)=a T_hBig)cdot A_a^u le sum_a (A_a^u)^2 = I, \] where the inequality uses that~T is a measurement and the last identity uses that~A is projective. Averaging over~u gives \[ sum_h H_h = E_u sum_h H_h^u le I, \] so H is also a submeasurement and therefore lies in~polysubmqd. Set \[ zeta_variance = 24mcdotBig(eps + delta + fracmdqBig). \] Lemma~ below is the technical transfer from the averaged family~H back to the sandwiched operators A^u_h(u)T_hA^u_h(u). We use it in the completeness, consistency, strong self-consistency, and boundedness estimates that follow. We now verify the four conclusions of Lemma~. Proof of . The completeness of~H is sum_h brapsi H_h ot I ketpsi &= E_u sum_h brapsi H^u_h ot I ketpsi notag\\ &= E_u sum_h brapsi bigl(A^u_h(u) cdot T_h cdot A^u_h(u)bigr) ot I ketpsi. Grouping the polynomials according to their value at~u gives E_u sum_h brapsi bigl(A^u_h(u) cdot T_h cdot A^u_h(u)bigr) ot I ketpsi = E_u sum_a brapsi bigl(A^u_a cdot T_[h(u) = a] cdot A^u_abigr) ot I ketpsi. We first move the leftmost copy of~A^u_a across the bipartition: approx_2sqrtdelta E_u sum_a brapsi bigl(T_[h(u)=a] cdot A^u_abigr) ot A^u_a ketpsi. The difference is bounded by Cauchy--Schwarz as in~; the first factor is at most sqrt2delta by self-consistency of~A, and the second is at most~1 because T_[h(u)=a] le I. We next remove the remaining copy of~A^u_a on Bob's side: approx_sqrtdelta E_u sum_a brapsi bigl(T_[h(u)=a] cdot A^u_abigr) ot I ketpsi. The first Cauchy--Schwarz factor is at most~1 because the fiber operators form a submeasurement after grouping~T by the value of~h(u). Here the second Cauchy--Schwarz factor is \[ E_u sum_aneq b brapsi A^u_a ot A^u_b ketpsi, \] which is at most~delta because~A is self-consistent and projective. Reindexing by~h and using~, \[ = sum_h brapsi bigl(T_h cdot E_u A^u_h(u)bigr) ot I ketpsi = sum_h brapsi (T_h cdot Z) ot I ketpsi = brapsi Z ot I ketpsi. \] Thus sum_h brapsi H_h ot I ketpsi geq brapsi Z ot I ketpsi - 3sqrtdelta. Since G is a measurement,~ and Lemma~ give \[ brapsi Z ot I ketpsi ge E_u sum_a brapsi A^u_a ot G_[g(u)=a] ketpsi ge 1-nu. \] Therefore the completeness is at least 1-nu-3sqrtdelta, which is bounded below by (1-nu)-zeta. Proof of . The inconsistency of~H with~A is E_u sum_a neq b brapsi A^u_a ot H_[h(u) = b] ketpsi = E_u sum_a, h: h(u) neq a brapsi A^u_a ot H_h ketpsi. The theorem-side off-diagonal selection used for this `add-in-u` application is , and the corresponding left/right scalar quantities are and . The selected scalar chain for this specialization is recorded by . Apply Lemma~ with mathcal O=F_q, M=A, and S_u=\(a,h):h(u)neq a\. Then \[ approx_4 sqrtzeta_variance E_u sum_a, h: h(u) neq a brapsi bigl(A^u_h(u) cdot A^u_a cdot A^u_h(u)bigr)ot T_h ketpsi, \] and the right-hand side is~0 because~A is projective. Hence E_u sum_a neq b brapsi A^u_a ot H_[h(u) = b] ketpsi leq 4 sqrtzeta_variance. Since \[ 4sqrtzeta_variance = 4 sqrt24 m cdotBig(eps + delta + fracmdqBig) le 20 m cdot Big(eps^1/2 + delta^1/2 + (d/q)^1/2Big) le zeta, \] this proves . Proof of . From the definition of H_h^u and the projectivity of~A, H^u_h &= A^u_h(u) cdot T_h cdot A^u_h(u) = A^u_h(u) cdot H^u_h cdot A^u_h(u), \\ A^u_h(u) cdot H^u_h' cdot A^u_h(u) &= H^u_h' cdot A^u_h(u) = bigl(A^u_h(u) cdot T_h' cdot A^u_h(u)bigr)cdot boneh(u) = h'(u). The strong self-consistency expression is sum_hinpolyfuncmqd brapsi H_h ot H_h ketpsi = E_u sum_h in polyfuncmqd brapsi H_h^u ot H_h ketpsi. Apply Lemma~ with mathcal O=polyfuncmqd, M=H, and S_u=\(h,h):hinpolyfuncmqd\. This gives approx_4 sqrtzeta_variance E_u sum_h in polyfuncmqd brapsi bigl(A^u_h(u) cdot H_h^u cdot A^u_h(u)bigr) ot T_h ketpsi. We next enlarge the sum from h'=h to all pairs h,h': approx_2sqrtzeta_variance + fracmdq E_u sum_h, h' in polyfuncmqd brapsi bigl(A^u_h(u) cdot H^u_h' cdot A^u_h(u)bigr) ot T_h ketpsi. The added off-diagonal contribution is - &= E_u sum_h neq h' brapsi bigl(A^u_h(u) cdot H^u_h' cdot A^u_h(u)bigr) ot T_h ketpsi notag\\ &= E_u sum_h neq h' brapsi bigl(A^u_h(u) cdot T_h' cdot A^u_h(u)bigr) ot T_h ketpsi cdot boneh(u) = h'(u), where the second equality is~. To estimate~, first replace the left copy of A^u_h(u) by A^v_h(v): approx_sqrtzeta_variance E_u,v sum_h neq h' brapsi bigl(A^v_h(v) cdot T_h' cdot A^u_h(u)bigr) ot T_h ketpsi cdot boneh(u) = h'(u). The corresponding Cauchy--Schwarz bound is Big|E_u,v sum_h neq h' brapsi bigl((A^u_h(u) - A^v_h(v)) cdot T_h' cdot A^u_h(u)bigr) ot T_h ketpsi cdot boneh(u) = h'(u)Big|\\ leq sqrtE_u,v sum_h neq h' brapsi bigl((A^u_h(u) - A^v_h(v)) cdot T_h' cdot (A^u_h(u) - A^v_h(v))bigr) ot T_hketpsi\\ cdot sqrtE_u,v sum_h neq h' brapsi bigl(A^u_h(u) cdot T_h' cdot A^u_h(u)bigr) ot T_hketpsi cdot boneh(u) = h'(u). The first factor is bounded by sqrtzeta_variance via Lemma~, and the second by~1 because T and H^u are submeasurements. Repeating the same argument for the remaining copy of~A yields approx_sqrtzeta_variance E_u,v sum_h neq h' brapsi bigl(A^v_h(v) cdot T_h' cdot A^v_h(v)bigr) ot T_h ketpsi cdot boneh(u) = h'(u). The same intermediate estimate gives E_u,v sum_h neq h' brapsi bigl(A^v_h(v) cdot T_h' cdot A^v_h(v)bigr)ot T_hketpsi leq 1, so Schwartz--Zippel bounds the indicator average by md/q and proves~. Using~, the right-hand side of~ is E_u sum_h, h' in polyfuncmqd brapsi bigl(H^u_h' cdot A^u_h(u)bigr) ot T_h ketpsi. Replace the remaining copy of A^u_h(u) by A^v_h(v): approx_sqrtzeta_variance E_u,v sum_h, h' in polyfuncmqd brapsi bigl(H^u_h' cdot A^v_h(v)bigr) ot T_h ketpsi. Here the first Cauchy--Schwarz factor is at most~1 because T and H^u are submeasurements, and the second is again bounded by Lemma~. Finally move this last copy of~A^v_h(v) to Bob's side: approx_sqrt2delta E_u,v sum_h, h' in polyfuncmqd brapsi H^u_h' ot bigl(T_h cdot A^v_h(v)bigr) ketpsi. Substituting~, then~, and finally the already proved bound~, one obtains \[ ge sum_h brapsi H_h ot I ketpsi - 4sqrtzeta_variance. \] Combining~, , , and~ gives \[ sum_h brapsi H_h ot H_h ketpsi ge sum_h brapsi H_h ot I ketpsi - 11 sqrtzeta_variance - sqrt2delta - fracmdq. \] The Lean formalization records this step as named internal bounds, starting with the structure and the exact residual-side expansion and then uses the proved lemma together with to recover the final helper-stage self-consistency conclusion. The theorem-level derivation is therefore not moved into an additional hypothesis. The paper's arithmetic shows that the right-hand error is at most \[ 57mcdot Big(eps^1/2 + delta^1/2 + (d/q)^1/2Big) le zeta, \] which proves . Proof of . The helper-stage boundedness quantity is \[ brapsi Z ot I ketpsi -E_u sum_a brapsi A^u_a ot H_[h(u)=a] ketpsi. \] The reindexing of the sum by~h is the algebraic identity \[ sum_a A^u_a ot H_[h(u)=a] = sum_h A^u_h(u) ot H_h, \] whose averaged scalar form reads \[ E_u sum_a brapsi\,A^u_a ot H_[h(u)=a]\,ketpsi = E_u sum_h brapsi\,A^u_h(u) ot H_h\,ketpsi. \] Using sum_a A_a^u=I, the pointwise difference between the right-placed total I ot H.total = sum_h I ot H_h and the helper-agreement operator at u reindexes as the off-diagonal sum \[ sum_h I ot H_h - sum_a A^u_a ot H_[h(u)=a] = sum_h sum_a neq h(u) A^u_a ot H_h, \] whose averaged scalar form reads \[ sum_h brapsi\,I ot H_h\,ketpsi - E_u sum_a brapsi\,A^u_a ot H_[h(u)=a]\,ketpsi = E_u sum_h sum_a neq h(u) brapsi\,A^u_a ot H_h\,ketpsi. \] Combined with~ this gives \[ brapsi Z ot I ketpsi -E_u sum_a brapsi A^u_a ot H_[h(u)=a] ketpsi le brapsi Z ot I ketpsi - sum_h brapsi I ot H_h ketpsi + 4 sqrtzeta_variance. \] By~, the right-hand side is at most 3sqrtdelta+4sqrtzeta_variance. Substituting the definition of zeta_variance and collecting terms gives \[ 23mcdotBig(eps^1/2 + delta^1/2 + (d/q)^1/2Big) le zeta. \] Together with~, this proves .

nodes.name: Explicit matrix feasible bounds
nodes.statement: In every concrete matrix realization, the uniform family \(T_g=(2|polyfuncmqd|)^-1I\) has total mass \((1/2)I\). The dual operator \(Z=2I\) dominates the identity and satisfies \(Z-A_ggeq I\), hence \(Zgeq A_g\), for every polynomial \(g\). In the canonical block SDP, the corresponding block matrix is feasible, its slack block is \((1/2)I\), and the canonical dual slack for the same dual witness also dominates the block identity. More generally, dual feasibility implies positivity of \(Z\), since the averaged point operators \(A_g\) are positive semidefinite.

nodes.name: Matrix slackness output
nodes.statement: From a matrix-level strong-duality witness with complementary slackness of the shape asserted by Lemma~, one obtains a complete measurement \(\T_g\\), a feasible dual operator \(Z\), equality of the primal and dual objectives, and the equations \(T_gZ=T_gA_g\) for all \(g\). Lean isolates the saturated canonical optimal-pair output required from strong duality: a feasible canonical primal matrix, a dual-feasible operator with equal objective value, canonical complementary slackness, and vanishing of the extra canonical slack block. This datum gives the matrix-level slackness-carrying SDP statement, whose witness is already a complete matrix measurement, and is then transported to the abstract Section~9 statement without assuming \(I le Z\). The displayed measurement witness is read directly from that abstract statement. The canonical saturation datum is now the only matrix-level input used to pass from strong duality to the abstract SDP statement. The paper-facing self-improvement helper consumes the resulting abstract SDP statement.
